title: Groundnut and Mushroom Luwombo
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Mushrooms and half a kilo of groundnut paste sealed into banana leaf parcels with onion, tomato, garlic and thirty grams of curry powder, and steamed an hour — the vegetarian luwombo.
longDesc: Luwombo is the ceremonial dish of Buganda, created in 1887 for Kabaka Mwanga II by his chef Kawuta, and it is usually made with chicken, beef or fish. This is the mushroom version, and it is not a modern substitution — mushroom luwombo is one of the standard fillings. The quantities here are unusually precise for a dish that is normally cooked by eye, and the thirty grams of curry powder is a real amount: two full tablespoons, which tells you how assertive this is meant to be.
ingredients: Banana leaves, wilted over a flame
Banana leaf spines, for the steaming rig
equipment: Deep pan with a tight lid
steps: Wilt the banana leaves briefly over a flame until they turn glossy and flexible.
Chop the onion, tomatoes and garlic. Clean the mushrooms.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water to a thick sauce.
Mix the mushrooms, onion, tomatoes, garlic, curry powder and salt into the groundnut sauce.
Spoon the mixture into the centre of each wilted leaf, leaving a border.
Fold the leaf into a parcel and tie it closed.
Set the parcels on a bed of banana leaf spines in the pan, with water below the spines.
Cover tightly and steam for about 1 hour.
Serve the parcels unopened, at the table.
chefTips: Wilt the leaves before folding. Unwilted banana leaf splits along the grain and the sauce escapes.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water. Hot water makes it seize, every time.
Thirty grams of curry powder is about two tablespoons and it is correct. Luwombo is a strongly flavoured dish.
Water below the spines and never touching the parcels — the rig described in UGA030.

An hour is what this source gives. Published luwombo times range from one hour to four across sources, which is a real and unresolved disagreement, so check the parcel rather than the clock if you are unsure.
Serve them closed. Opening a luwombo at the table is the whole ceremony of it.
Mushroom luwombo is not a vegetarian substitution invented later — it is one of the standard fillings alongside chicken, beef and fish.
Termite flour prepared as luwombo, per UGA062, is another traditional filling, and the same sauce and parcel method applies.
commonMistakes: Dissolving the groundnut paste in hot water.
Reducing the curry powder to a teaspoon.
Water high enough to boil the parcels.
Opening the parcels in the kitchen.
sources: Adapted from 'Groundnut and Mushroom Luwombo', p17 of 'Traditional Products and Dishes: Uganda — From Earth to Table', second edition 2018, Slow Food International — the 250 g of mushrooms, 500 g of groundnut paste, 1 onion, 3 tomatoes, 2 garlic cloves, 30 g of curry powder, 1 teaspoon of salt and the roughly one-hour steam are all as printed there.

That booklet also prints a Beef Luwombo on p34 giving 100 g of salt against 500 g of beef. That is a 20 per cent salt ratio and inedible; it is almost certainly a misprint, and it is recorded here as a warning rather than used.
The 1887 origin for Kabaka Mwanga II by his chef Kawuta, and the one-to-four-hour spread in published steaming times, are documented separately from the booklet.
The banana leaf and spine steaming rig is from UGA030.
storage: Refrigerate in the parcels up to 3 days.
reheating: Steam the parcels again for 10 minutes.
healthBenefits: Groundnut paste is high in plant protein, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
Mushrooms add B vitamins, selenium and, with no meat in the dish, most of its savoury depth.
Steamed in leaf with no added fat at all beyond what is in the groundnuts.
culturalNote: That the most ceremonial dish in Buganda has a standard vegetarian version, and has had one all along, is worth saying plainly — luwombo is defined by the leaf and the sauce, not by the meat. The dish is named for its vessel, like kikalayi, which is a habit worth noticing in Ugandan naming.
